### Question 1

Think about the difference between a raincoat and a roof. A roof is built into the building and protects everyone underneath it without anyone doing anything — that is an engineering control, like a ventilation system or a sharps container. A raincoat only works if you put it on, and it only protects the person wearing it. PPE is the raincoat: gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection that you personally wear so contaminants land on the gear instead of on your skin, clothes, eyes, nose, or mouth. Two things that fool people: being throwaway does not make something PPE (a disposable bedpan is not PPE), and a sterile drape over a surgical site is not PPE either, because that barrier is protecting the patient, not you.

### Question 2

Getting dressed for a snowstorm follows the same logic: coat first, then hat and goggles, then mittens last — because you need working fingers to zip the coat and adjust the strap behind your head. If you put the mittens on first, you would be fumbling with everything else while those mittens repeatedly brush your face. PPE works the same way, with one bonus reason: gloves get pulled up over the gown's wrist cuffs so no bare skin shows at the seam, and you cannot do that if the gloves went on first.

### Question 3

Imagine painting a wall while wearing an old shirt. Where does the paint land? All over the front and the arms — not on your back, and not on the inside of the shirt. A gown works the same way: everything you leaned toward, reached across, and touched hit the front and sleeves. So when you take it off, you deliberately reach for the parts that never faced the patient — the ties in back and the inside surface — and peel it away from you, rolling it so the messy side ends up folded in on itself instead of brushing your uniform.

### Question 4

Think of taping a box for shipping. If you run tape down the middle but leave a half-inch gap at one corner, water gets in through that corner — it does not matter how strong the rest of the tape is. Your wrist is that corner: it is where the glove ends and the gown begins. Pulling the glove up over the gown cuff overlaps the two pieces, the way you overlap two strips of tape, so there is no open seam. And the gown cuff itself is usually soft knit fabric, exactly the kind of material you do not want wicking body fluid and holding it against your skin.

### Question 5

Getting fit tested is like going to a shoe store and having someone measure your foot to learn you are a size 8 wide in that specific brand. You do not re-measure every morning, but you do check that the shoe is actually on right and laced before you run. That quick check is the user seal check: you cover the respirator, inhale and exhale, and feel whether air leaks around the edges. Measuring happens before your first use and at least once a year after that; the quick check happens every single time you put it on, because air always takes the easy path — if there is a gap at the edge, that is where it goes instead of through the filter.

### Question 6

Picture taking a hot pan out of the oven. You do not grab the pan — you grab the handle, because the handle is the part that is safe to hold. Every piece of PPE has a designated handle: for a face shield it is the headband behind your head, for goggles the earpieces, for a gown the ties, for gloves the cuff. The front of the shield is the part that caught the splashes, so touching it moves whatever landed there onto your fingers. Those fingers then travel up to your mask, right next to your eyes, nose, and mouth — exactly the trip you spent the whole encounter preventing.

### Question 7

Compare a window screen to a diving mask. A window screen keeps insects and splashing rain out, and it is good at that, but air moves freely around and through it. A diving mask has to press tightly against your face, because even a small gap is where water comes in. A surgical mask is the screen: it catches droplets and splashes flying at your mouth and nose. An N95 is the diving mask: it must seal, so the air you breathe is forced through the filter material instead of slipping around the edges. That is also why only the N95 needs fit testing — a screen does not have to match your face, but a seal does.

### Question 8

Gloves work like paper towels, not like oven mitts. You use a paper towel for one mess and throw it away — you would not wipe up something soiled and then dry a clean dish with that same towel. Providing perineal care and then touching an open dressing with the same gloves carries organisms straight from the dirtiest site to the one most vulnerable to infection. Sanitizer does not rescue the situation either: it was designed and tested for skin, not for glove material, and it can weaken the glove while the soil stays sitting on the surface. New task in a cleaner spot means new gloves, and clean hands in between.

### Question 9

Choosing PPE is like dressing for a forecast. A windbreaker handles drizzle, but if the forecast says downpour you want something water cannot soak through, plus something over your face. A standard isolation gown is the windbreaker — it wets through when real fluid volume hits it. A fluid-resistant gown is the rain slicker. Your eyes, nose, and mouth are wet, open doorways for organisms, so when a splash is expected all three need covering: the face shield guards the eyes, the mask underneath guards the nose and mouth. Notice that you built this choice from what you expect to hit you, not from anything written in the patient's chart.

### Question 10

Regular eyeglasses are like holding an umbrella straight out in front of you during a windy storm — rain still arrives from the sides and over the top. Goggles behave more like a helmet visor: they wrap around and close those gaps, so a splash coming in at an angle still cannot reach your eyes. Your eyes matter here because their moist surface is an entry route for organisms, just like your nose and mouth. And goggles cover only the eyes, so a mask still goes on underneath — each piece of gear does one job, and you have to cover every doorway you expect to be hit.

### Question 11

Compare two ways of keeping people from being hurt by a hole in a sidewalk. You could fill in the hole, and then nobody can fall in, ever, whether or not they are paying attention. Or everyone walking past could wear knee pads. The knee pads genuinely help, but the hole is still there, and they only work if every person remembers them, has the right size, and puts them on correctly, every single day. PPE is the knee pads. Ranking it last is not a claim that it is weak or optional — it is a claim about reliability: it protects one person at a time and can fail the moment someone is rushed, tired, undertrained, or handed the wrong size.

### Question 12

Picture a pair of muddy boots. Extended use is keeping them on the whole time you move between four different garden beds — your hands never touch the muddy outside. Reuse is pulling them off between each bed and tugging them back on again, and every one of those cycles puts your fingers on the dirty part and shifts how they sit. That is exactly why extended use is usually the safer of the two: fewer chances to touch a contaminated surface, and fewer chances to disturb the seal. Neither one is the everyday plan — hospitals reach for extended use first when supplies get tight, and only fall back on reuse when they get much tighter. And one rule never bends: a respirator is fitted to one specific face, so it is never passed to a coworker, no matter how short supplies get.
